newsitem.title: UK: Risk securitisation model needs refining - insurers.
newsitem.headline: Risk securitisation model needs refining - insurers.

text.p: A series of risk securitisation deals in the last few weeks does not mean that the insurance industry has found the right template for the future, senior company officials told a conference on Tuesday.
Philip Martin, a director at Sedgwick Insurance Strategy Group, said: "There has been a lot of expectation of the benefits of securitisation over an unrealistic time frame."
"We are not there yet, there is a lot of work to be done," he said.

Martin said the bond offering from Texas-based insurance group USAA which closed last week ahead of schedule was an important benchmark, as were similar placements by St Paul SPC.N and Winterthur WINZn.S.
"The Winterthur placement was not high risk or high return but it was the first to be publicly placed and over-subscribed so it was a landmark," he said.

Martin also pointed to some of the drawbacks of securitisation including a high level of complexity, high set up costs, and the question as to whether the types of risk covered are too severe for investors.

Other issues with securitisation raised at the Institute of International Research conference on alternative risk financing included the regulatory framework and legal questions which have yet to be solved as well as the rating of the bonds.
Gail Belonsky, vice president of Swiss Re Financial Products said overcoming the regulatory process in the United States is gradually becoming easier but it can still take a long time.
Katherine Coates, a partner at Clifford Chance, said there was still some doubt in the UK as to whether insurance companies can legally use derivatives.
Insurance companies are restricted to carrying out insurance company business and although the issue has been discussed in the Court of Appeal no agreement was reached.
Despite the drawbacks companies such as Swiss Re are determined to push on with the development of securitisation.
"Swiss Re see this as something that is going to be important in the future," Belonsky said.
